rates=(0.49,0.51)

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful auditing problem: multiclass equalized odds must account for different types of misclassification, and individual-level data may be unavailable. Extending Sabato and Yom-Tov (2020) to this setting provides a useful contribution with an interpretable, population-weighted mixture formulation.

For exact population statistics, Theorem 4.1 gives a sound characterization of multiclass DCP. The efficiently computable lower bound in Eq. (7), together with feasible baseline assignments providing upper bounds, offers a useful way to assess approximation quality. Monotonicity under label merging also motivates the greedy initialization.

The experiments cover decision trees, nearest-neighbor classifiers, and neural networks on Census and Natality data. Greedy initialization followed by local optimization substantially improves the reported alternatives, and several known-confusion-matrix intervals are very tight, particularly in Tables 4 and 6. Pseudocode, algorithmic appendices, and a public code link support inspection.
weaknesses: The central accuracy claim for aggregate-only auditing is not demonstrated. Although Section 7 claims small upper/lower-bound gaps in both regimes, Tables 2 and 7–10 report local optimizer values without corresponding lower bounds on minDCP. An upper bound on minDCP cannot certify a lower bound on the actual classifier's DCP. Showing that this optimizer value falls below the actual classifier's DCP interval does not establish proximity to the minimum. Consequently, the accuracy of this component and the interpretation of the election/education trends remain insufficiently supported.

The robustness assertions in Sections 4 and 7.1 do not follow from DCP being a population fraction and are false under total-variation error. Already in the binary special case, take two equally weighted groups with conditional prediction rates 0.5 for every true class. Perturb these rates to 0.49 and 0.51 across the groups: the joint distribution changes by total variation 0.01, while DCP increases from zero to approximately 0.01961. A stated error metric and an actual stability analysis are needed. Similarly, clipping confusion matrices and smoothing prediction marginals change the optimization target; their effects on certificates for the original inputs are not quantified.

Appendix D contains a concrete error in its convergence argument. The surrogate in Eq. (18) is not jointly convex: on the branch b < a, it equals a² − ab, whose Hessian [[2, −1], [−1, 0]] is indefinite. Both arguments are optimized in Eq. (15), so the claimed convex benchmark underlying Figure 4 is invalid. The applicability of the cited SLP convergence results to the implemented constraint-removal and step-selection rules also needs justification. This does not invalidate every feasible upper bound, but it weakens the algorithmic guarantees.

The optimization evaluation lacks independent solver comparisons, runtime/scaling measurements, and small instances with known global optima. Even the simple identity-baseline bound DCP ≤ classification error is omitted: it improves the eight-class decision-tree result in Table 1 from 23.61% to 22.61%. Some reported intervals remain substantial, such as 8.29%–23.61%, so the broad accuracy claims need qualification. Stronger benchmarks would establish when the proposed optimization is practically advantageous.

Smaller presentation and reproducibility gaps include unnamed Census prediction targets, unspecified preprocessing and train/test protocols, and incomplete experimental initialization and stopping settings for aggregate optimization. These are fixable reporting issues; the principal reasons for weak rejection are the missing aggregate-setting validation and the unsupported robustness and convergence claims.
